evidence: Read the whole context first (section 'It feels fake', heading plus four paragraphs), then the draft, 'Have you got any sense of what it is that's making it feel fake?', then SOURCE ('Do you have a sense of what it is that feels fake?', meaning from his guide: 'First ask what feels fake: the wording, the image, the expectation, or the role you're trying to perform'). DOES WHAT THE_CHANGE SAYS: the one question is swapped for Emulate's sample-co wording and nothing else in the paragraph is touched; the draft appears once in the context. MEANING: it sits right under the heading as the section's first move, so 'First ask' is kept by position, and the four candidates (the words, an image, what you are expecting to get from this, a role you feel you have to play) stay in the next sentence unchanged. The only shift is 'what feels fake' to 'what is making it feel fake' (the thing itself to the cause of the feeling). I checked that the unchanged list answers both readings, and it fits the draft slightly better, because 'what you are expecting to get from this' can make a practice feel fake but can't itself feel fake. No claim, fact, first-person detail, study or name is added. 'it' is the practice, anchored by the heading 'It feels fake' and by the next sentence's 'this', the same referent the source used. SEAM CHECK: the question reads as a person asking, not as a bridge or a summary. 'Have you got' sits with the section's existing British-leaning idiom ('see how you get on' in the last paragraph). The straight apostrophe in 'that's' matches the straight ones around it (doesn't, don't, isn't); no stray spaces or odd punctuation. It does not sound like a different writer from the sentences after it. Outside the draft: the unchanged third paragraph has one curly apostrophe (aren’t) among otherwise straight ones; it is not part of this change, so I did not count it against the draft. TELL ROWS: went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on the literal draft in its paragraph and found no row PRESENT. The ones I pressed hardest: T15 (words swapped for less likely ones): 'Do you have a sense' to 'Have you got any sense' is a shift of register, not a thesaurus swap, and a 14-word question has no other tell for the swap to leave standing. T24 and T19 (question answered straight away, announcing setup): the question is followed at once by its candidate answers, but that structure is the source's own, it is the question a reader under a heading 'It feels fake' would actually be asking, and the list is prompts, not manufactured suspense. T02 and T22 (manual cadence, coach register): the paragraph's ask, list, reassure, instruct cadence is the unchanged text; the draft adds one question, not reassurance. T26: 'fake' and 'feel' repeat the heading's topic and anchor it. T13 and T09 (asked for by the D9 note): the surrounding paragraph's counterexample (it is not necessarily about lacking a grown-up voice or resisting the work) and its asides are untouched, and a single question has no weight to equalise. LINTER: 'D9 follows the source order' accepted: one sentence replaces one sentence, so the order is given, and T13 and T09 are answered above. 'E36/E41 heavy second person' ('7.1 you per 100 of my words') accepted: it is one 'you' in a 14-word question, the same single 'you' the replaced sentence had, so the change adds no second-person weight and the rate is an artifact of a one-sentence sample.
